question: Within the broad nonconvergent-but-nondivergent range commonly called a large learning rate, which initial rates actually prepare a network for the best later fine-tuning or stochastic weight averaging?

key_findings.claim: Only the lower portion of the chaotic-equilibrium learning-rate regime consistently prepares high-generalization solutions; increasing the initial rate within the same nominal regime eventually reverses the benefit.
key_findings.evidence: Across the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 learning-rate sweep, fine-tuning and stochastic weight averaging improve beyond every converged first-regime solution after pre-training in the authors' subregime 2A, but degrade through subregime 2B and can become worse than training from scratch. The appendix reports the same ordering for ConvNet on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, with weaker effects for the simpler ConvNet.

key_findings.claim: The geometry of downstream solutions changes across the large-rate range: lower chaotic rates locate one connected high-quality basin, whereas higher rates expose diverse and increasingly worse minima.
key_findings.evidence: For subregime 2A, solutions obtained with different fine-tuning rates have similar accuracy, small angular separation, and low linear-path barriers; SWA is farther away but remains linearly connected. Through subregime 2B, fine-tuned solutions separate in accuracy and angular distance and eventually in train-error connectivity, while SWA quality deteriorates.

key_findings.claim: A single abrupt learning-rate drop is the source of much of subregime 2B's damage; inserting an intermediate lower chaotic rate nearly restores the best quality.
key_findings.evidence: The two-step appendix schedule pre-trains at a high subregime-2B rate, spends 200 epochs at a lower subregime-2A rate, and then fine-tunes another 200 epochs in regime 1. Figure 7 shows this path recovering almost the accuracy obtained by beginning directly in subregime 2A for both the lowest and highest fine-tuning rates.

key_findings.claim: The narrow-rate conclusion survives a conventional ResNet-18 training configuration, although the clean three-regime interpretation does not.
key_findings.evidence: With ordinary whole-space SGD, momentum, weight decay, and CIFAR augmentation, the best fine-tuned and averaged models again come from slightly inside the second regime, not from its full width. Both methods approach the approximately 95% CIFAR-10 accuracy associated with a standard schedule, while SWA rapidly worsens and fine-tuning becomes solution-dependent at larger initial rates.

key_findings.claim: Very large divergent-regime pre-training can sometimes improve later low-rate optimization without learning a useful predictor, but the proposed explanation is correlational.
key_findings.evidence: After regime-3 pre-training, low-rate fine-tuning outperforms training from the standard initialization. The authors show that scale-invariant parameter-group norms become widely dispersed, so some groups receive larger effective rates; this difference persists after low-rate fine-tuning and mostly disappears after high-rate fine-tuning. No intervention equalizes the norm distribution to establish causality.

method.core_idea: Make effective learning rate controllable by training fully scale-invariant networks on a fixed-radius sphere, sweep initial rates across convergence, chaotic equilibrium, and divergence, and judge each pre-trained point by downstream fine-tuning and weight averaging rather than its immediate accuracy.
method.mechanism: The authors freeze the last layer, remove trainable batch-normalization parameters, and apply projected SGD so a fixed nominal rate is also a fixed rate on the unit sphere. After 200 epochs at each pre-training rate, they either train 200 epochs with a convergent fine-tuning rate or average consecutive checkpoints while continuing at the same rate. They compare test accuracy, angular distance, and train/test linear-path barriers, replicate over two architectures and two CIFAR datasets, then repeat the central sweep in a conventional ResNet-18 setup with momentum, weight decay, and augmentation.
assumptions: Projected optimization of a fully scale-invariant network is a useful controlled model for learning-rate behavior in ordinary normalized networks.
Two hundred epochs is sufficient for pre-training dynamics to stabilize and for every selected fine-tuning rate to converge.
The empirical regime boundaries inferred from accuracy and loss dynamics are stable enough to support the 2A/2B subdivision.
Linear interpolation barriers and angular distance in parameter space meaningfully characterize whether downstream solutions occupy the same basin.
CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 with ConvNet and ResNet-18 capture enough architectural diversity to motivate, but not prove, a general learning-rate prescription.

techniques.role: Fixes scale-invariant weights to a sphere so the swept learning rate does not drift through changing parameter norms.
Separates the effect of an initial pre-training rate from the convergent rate used to reach a final solution.
Tests whether checkpoints sampled at the initial rate occupy a region whose center generalizes well without an explicit rate drop.
Measures train- and test-error barriers along straight parameter interpolations to distinguish shared low-error regions from separate minima.
Uses the norm distribution of scale-invariant groups to diagnose why nominally low-rate fine-tuning can behave differently after divergent pre-training.

evaluations.setting: Scale-invariant ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10; 200 pre-training epochs followed by 200 fine-tuning epochs, or SWA of subsequent checkpoints
evaluations.metric: Final test accuracy across pre-training and fine-tuning rates
evaluations.result: The optimum lies in a narrow lower-chaotic subregime 2A; quality declines across higher-chaotic subregime 2B
evaluations.baseline: Best fixed-rate regime-1 training from random initialization and immediate drops from other pre-training rates

evaluations.metric: Angular distance and linear train/test-error barriers among low-rate, high-rate, and SWA endpoints
evaluations.result: Subregime-2A endpoints are close or linearly connected; subregime-2B endpoints grow apart and eventually lose train-error connectivity
evaluations.baseline: Geometry of endpoints reached from the same pre-trained checkpoint at lower initial rates

evaluations.setting: ConvNet on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100
evaluations.metric: Final test-accuracy profiles over initial rates
evaluations.result: All three preserve the lower-second-regime optimum; ConvNet shows a smaller improvement and weaker high-rate degradation

evaluations.setting: Training fixed-rate spherical models near the regime-1/2 boundary until loss reaches 10^-3, capped at 20,000 epochs
evaluations.metric: Epochs to convergence and final test accuracy
evaluations.result: Convergence time rises sharply beyond the 200-epoch boundary, while converged minima approach the corresponding fine-tuned accuracy
evaluations.baseline: Two-stage pre-training plus fine-tuning, which reaches the region within the prescribed stage budgets

evaluations.setting: Conventional ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 with SGD momentum 0.9, weight decay 5x10^-4, and standard crop/flip augmentation
evaluations.metric: Fine-tuned and SWA test accuracy over initial rate
evaluations.result: Both peak slightly inside the second regime and approach approximately 95% test accuracy; higher initial rates degrade SWA and diversify fine-tuned endpoints
evaluations.baseline: Approximately 95% test accuracy from a conventional standard learning-rate schedule

limitations: Author-stated: the clearest analysis alters the network by fixing the final layer, removing trainable batch-normalization parameters, and constraining weights to a sphere.
Author-stated: only the first two regimes are visible in the conventional setup, and augmentation makes even their boundary approximate.
Author-stated: effects are weaker for the simpler ConvNet, and ResNet-18/CIFAR-100 exhibits periodic dynamics that destabilize SWA beyond ten checkpoints.

Reviewer-identified: the paper provides figures rather than tabulated sweep values and uncertainty intervals, making the width and run-to-run stability of the proposed sweet spot difficult to quantify.

Reviewer-identified: dataset coverage is limited to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; there are no transformers, language tasks, adaptive optimizers, large-batch regimes, or modern large-scale training recipes.
Reviewer-identified: regime thresholds depend on architecture, normalization, radius, batch size, and budget, so the work supplies a diagnostic procedure rather than a portable numeric learning rate.
Reviewer-identified: the loss-bowl and parameter-norm explanations are interpretations of geometry and correlations, not causally isolated mechanisms.
failure_modes: Treating every nonconvergent stable learning rate as beneficial can select subregime 2B, where an abrupt rate drop yields worse endpoints than training from scratch.
A nominal learning rate can cease to identify the true optimization regime when scale-invariant parameter norms drift.
SWA can average checkpoints from different low-loss regions under periodic or high-rate dynamics and thereby reduce accuracy.
An overly long high-rate phase can erase the basin-location advantage even while training remains below outright divergence.
A regime boundary estimated at one training budget can move when the budget, augmentation, normalization, or optimizer changes.
Parameter-space linear connectivity can disagree between train and test errors and need not imply functional equivalence.
reusable_insights: Evaluate an initial optimization phase by the quality reachable after a standardized readout phase, not only by its current loss or accuracy.
Search learning rates densely near the transition into nonconvergent dynamics; a log-wide category called 'large' can hide opposite downstream effects.
When an aggressive initial rate harms a direct drop, test a short intermediate-rate bridge before discarding the checkpoint.
Control effective rather than nominal learning rate when normalization makes parameter scale non-identifiable.
Combine endpoint performance with connectivity and distance probes to distinguish one robust basin from multiple schedule-sensitive minima.
open_questions: Can online statistics identify the 2A-to-2B transition without running a full downstream sweep?
Does the narrow beneficial interval persist for transformers, language modeling, adaptive optimizers, or billion-parameter scale?
Which intervention on parameter-group norms would causally test the proposed regime-3 initialization mechanism?
How do batch size, data augmentation, weight decay, and pre-training duration jointly move the regime boundaries?
Can a rate controller optimize for downstream basin quality rather than instantaneous loss descent?

competitive_landscape.title: Training Scale-Invariant Neural Networks on the Sphere Can Happen in Three Regimes
competitive_landscape.difference: Kodryan et al. introduce spherical optimization and the convergence/chaotic-equilibrium/divergence taxonomy; this paper uses that controlled system to subdivide the chaotic regime according to the quality reachable after fine-tuning or averaging.

competitive_landscape.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: Lewkowycz et al. derive solvable catapult dynamics and predict a narrow stable large-rate phase associated with flatter minima; the present work empirically resolves downstream quality within the broader chaotic spherical regime and contrasts immediate drops with SWA.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD with Large Step Sizes Learns Sparse Features
competitive_landscape.difference: Andriushchenko et al. argue that large steps stabilize loss and induce stochastic dynamics toward sparse features, emphasizing how long that phase is maintained; this paper instead maps initial-rate location to downstream basin quality and exposes a harmful high-chaotic subregime.

competitive_landscape.title: Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates
competitive_landscape.difference: Smith and Topin advocate a one-cycle schedule with a large maximum rate for fast training across several vision models; this paper warns that the useful initial interval is narrow and studies endpoint geometry rather than end-to-end speed.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that the initial large-learning-rate range yielding optimal later fine-tuning or weight averaging is substantially narrower than standard guidance suggests.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Dense spherical sweeps separate the chaotic regime into beneficial 2A and harmful 2B regions, use connectivity and angular geometry to characterize their endpoints, reproduce the ordering across four architecture/dataset settings, and recover the central pattern in conventional ResNet-18 training.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Relative to phase-transition, catapult, super-convergence, and sparse-feature accounts, the distinctive contribution is a downstream-utility map within the nominal large-rate regime plus the finding that a single intermediate drop can rescue an overly aggressive start. Its generality beyond small vision benchmarks remains untested.

reviewer_notes: Findings and quantitative setup details were checked against all nine extracted pages. Most performance comparisons are author-reported from curves rather than tables; approximate values are labeled accordingly. Competitor metadata and versions were checked on primary arXiv, PMLR, and NeurIPS records on 2026-08-23. Mechanistic language about bowls, sparse features, and norm dispersion is treated as hypothesis unless an intervention is reported.
